passage:
Running club notes. Saurabh Joshi, coach. Saturday, 18 January
Sonali has run with the Saturday group since last April. At first she needed a reminder every Friday night. Now I don't think she even decides; she just turns up at 6:15, stretches by the same lamppost and asks who's pacing.
In December she missed three Saturdays while her father was in hospital. I half expected her to drop off, as many do. Instead she came back on the fourth, ran an easy 4 km at the back and said, "Felt weird not running. Like skipping brushing my teeth." She didn't apologise or promise to make up the distance.
She mentioned she expects to miss more when her new job starts in March. "I'll just come back when I can," she said, and went to find her water bottle.
What I did next: moved her to the easier group for two weeks without comment, and noted a check-in for March.

qa.q: How many Saturdays did Sonali miss in December?
qa.a: She missed three Saturdays.

qa.q: What does Sonali's 'Like skipping brushing my teeth' reveal about how running feels to her now?
qa.a: She feels uncomfortable when she misses a run, like skipping brushing her teeth, so running now needs little thought and is an ordinary part of her life.

qa.q: How did the coach support Sonali's return, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Saurabh moved her to an easier group for two weeks without comment and planned a March check-in, letting her come back without drama.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel seeing Sonali return?
qa.a: Saurabh half expected her to drop off, as many do, so the calm return is likely a relief and a sign the habit has taken root.

grounding: Shows a running habit that has become automatic after months, with the runner expecting lapses and returning calmly after a disruption.

passage:
Thursday, 9 pm
Back on the cycle today after nine days. The house shifting swallowed everything: boxes, the broker, the new gas connection, Usha's mother visiting. The cycle sat in the new building's parking under a bedsheet.
Funny thing is, I didn't sit down and plan a restart. This morning I just found myself pumping the tyres before chai, as if my hands had decided. Eight months ago I needed three alarms and a pep talk to do this ride.
The new route is longer, past the lake and under the flyover. My legs were heavy but I didn't mind much.
All nine days felt slightly off, like I'd forgotten something. Usha said I was grumpy. Probably true.
I know there'll be more gaps. Her sister's wedding in May, for one. Fine. The cycle will be there.
Vishal

qa.q: How many days was Vishal off the cycle?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: How did the nine days without cycling feel to Vishal, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: They felt slightly off and left Vishal grumpy, like something was forgotten, which suggests cycling has become a background habit that feels strange to skip.

qa.q: What in Vishal's attitude helps the habit survive future gaps?
qa.a: Vishal expects gaps like the May wedding and plans simply to return, instead of treating a break as failure.

qa.q: How might Usha have experienced those nine days?
qa.a: Usha, busy with the move and her mother's visit, found Vishal grumpy, and may be glad to see the cycle back in use.

grounding: Illustrates a months-old cycling habit that returns almost automatically after a house move, with future lapses expected and accepted.

passage:
In Buenos Aires, Santiago's alarm went off at 6:30, and he found himself in his running shoes before he'd really decided anything. Eight months of morning runs. It needed about as much thought as brushing his teeth.
On the last Saturday of the month, Esther asked him to skip it for a family breakfast. He did. That evening he felt strange, restless, like he'd forgotten something.
On Sunday, he just went again.
"You're not annoyed you missed one?" Esther asked.
"No. Sometimes life happens," he shrugged, tying his laces. "It just felt odd, not running. That's how I know it's mine now."

qa.q: How long had Santiago been running in the mornings?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What did Santiago feel on the evening after skipping his run?
qa.a: He felt strange and restless, like he'd forgotten something, showing the habit had become automatic.

qa.q: What makes Santiago's response to the missed run healthy?
qa.a: He expected occasional lapses and simply went again the next day without drama.

qa.q: How might Esther feel about his relaxed attitude?
qa.a: Esther seems pleased and perhaps surprised that he wasn't annoyed about skipping for the family.

grounding: Shows a young man for whom running has become automatic and odd to skip, returning without drama after a planned lapse.

passage:
In the office at the logistics company, Anand filled his water bottle at 11 and 3 every day, and did five minutes of stretching by the window. Tarun had watched him do it for months.
"Don't you ever forget?" Tarun asked.
"Not really. Feels weird when I don't. Like my back is waiting."
"You didn't do it last week."
"The audit was on. Three days I forgot completely." Anand shrugged. "Then on Monday I just started again. It's not a big deal any more."
Tarun looked at his own coffee mug and aching shoulders. "Show me the stretches?"
"Five minutes. Come."

qa.q: At what times does Anand fill his water bottle?
qa.a: At 11 and 3 every day.

qa.q: What does Anand mean when he says his back is waiting?
qa.a: He feels the stretching is so automatic that skipping it feels odd, and he is calm, not anxious, about it.

qa.q: What does Anand's response to the audit week show?
qa.a: That a settled habit survives lapses; he expected them and simply started again on Monday.

qa.q: What is Tarun feeling when he asks to see the stretches?
qa.a: Tarun seems curious and inspired, perhaps aware of his own aching shoulders.

grounding: Shows a young worker whose stretching habit has become background, returning without fuss after a busy audit week.

passage:
Kishore bhai,
You asked if I still do the Hindi reading every night. The funny thing is, I hardly think about it any more. It's been a year. I read a page before bed like I plug in my phone. If I skip it, the night feels unfinished.
I did miss a whole week in December, at my cousin's wedding in Jaipur. The old me would have panicked. This time I didn't even notice until the train home. Then I just picked up the book again that night. No drama. It's part of me now, not a project.
How's your guitar going?
Hrithik

qa.q: How long has Hrithik been reading Hindi every night?
qa.a: A year.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel about missing a week in December?
qa.a: Hrithik felt calm, not panicked, and simply picked up the book again that night.

qa.q: What shows that the habit has become background?
qa.a: It needs little thought, skipping feels unfinished, and a lapse doesn't cause drama.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel reading this?
qa.a: Kishore may feel encouraged and a little impressed, perhaps thinking about his own guitar habit.

grounding: Shows a young person whose reading habit has become automatic and odd to skip, returning calmly after a week's lapse.

passage: "You asked if I still do the morning stretches, Irawati. Honestly, I don't even think of it as a habit anymore. It's like brushing my teeth. Alarm, water, ten minutes of stretches on the rug, then chai. Eight months now. Last month we went to my cousin's wedding in Nagpur: three days, no rug, a room full of aunties. I didn't do them at all. The first morning back home, I just did them. No guilt, no big restart speech. It actually felt a bit uneasy on the days I skipped, like leaving the house without my watch. I'm sure I'll miss again sometime, when work gets mad or someone's ill. That's fine. I know the way back now. Remember the old Vinita, who quit everything in week three?"

qa.q: How long has Vinita been doing the morning stretches?
qa.a: Eight months now.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel on the days the stretches were skipped?
qa.a: Vinita felt a bit uneasy, like leaving the house without a watch, rather than guilty.

qa.q: What does Vinita's return after the wedding show?
qa.a: Returning the first morning back, with no guilt or restart speech, keeps a slip from turning into a stop.

qa.q: How might Irawati see the change in Vinita?
qa.a: Irawati, who knew the old Vinita who quit in week three, may be impressed at how settled the habit has become.

grounding: Shows a habit that has become background after months, feels odd to skip, and is resumed without drama after a disruption.
